title: Which auction rule pays the seller most?
hook: Make the winner pay their own bid, not the runner-up's. Surely the seller earns more?

knows: second-price bidders bid their true value
doesNotKnow: that with equilibrium bidding, first-price, second-price and even all-pay auctions earn the seller the same on average

misconception: Making winners pay their own bid must earn the seller more than charging the second-highest bid.
objective: The learner can explain that each rule changes how much bidders bid, so a higher price paid by one bidder (second-price), a lower price paid by the winner (first-price) and small bids paid by everyone (all-pay) all average the same for the seller.

claims.text: In 20,000 simulated auctions the seller averages $33.4 under second-price, $33.3 under first-price and $33.3 under all-pay.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: mulberry32(97), auction i takes values 100·r() for bidder A then B; seed 97 is the brief's, not chosen by the builder for the result. Totals over 20,000: 33.395 (second-price), 33.303 (first-price, bid v/2), 33.302 (all-pay, bid v²/200). Re-run in node by the builder (ncm-e02); matches the brief's check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own re-implementation (mulberry32(97), values 100 r() A then B): 33.395 / 33.303 / 33.302, shown to one decimal as 33.4 / 33.3 / 33.3.

claims.text: Theory gives $100 ÷ 3, about $33.3, for all three rules with two bidders and values uniform on $0 to $100: on average the seller collects the lower of the two values.
With these values, the optimal bids are: second-price, your value (the winner pays the lower value); first-price, half your value; all-pay, value squared ÷ 200, paid by both bidders.
claims.source: Symmetric equilibria for two bidders with values U(0,100): second-price truthful bidding is dominant; first-price b(v) = v/2; all-pay b(v) = v²/200 (all-pay bid = expected payment of a bidder with value v: v·(v/100) − ∫₀^v (x/100) dx = v²/200). Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 9 for first- and second-price. Fact-checker confirms. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node best-response check at v = 60: first-price best bid 30.00 (v/2) against v/2 bidding; all-pay best bid 18.000 = 60^2/200 against v^2/200. Second-price truthful is dominant (standard). Note: the builder's source text says 'Fact-checker confirms' before any check; that phrase is the builder's, not this pass's.

claims.text: Each rule changes how much bidders bid, and the changes cancel, so the seller's average is the same.
claims.source: Revenue equivalence for standard auctions with independent private values: R. B. Myerson, 'Optimal auction design', Math. Oper. Res. 6 (1981); J. G. Riley and W. F. Samuelson, Am. Econ. Rev. 71 (1981); Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 9. Fact-checker confirms attribution. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Holds for this model by c2/c3. Myerson, Math. Oper. Res. 6(1):58-73 (1981) and Riley & Samuelson, AER 71(3):381-392 (1981) confirmed as publications by search-result text only (not opened); their revenue-equivalence attribution is from my own knowledge. Easley-Kleinberg ch. 9 (auctions) placement matches my knowledge.

claims.text: This is a model: two bidders, values independent and uniform, everyone bidding optimally.
claims.source: Lesson framing; stage chip 'Model: 2 bidders · values random $0–100 · seed 97'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Framing; chip 'Model: 2 bidders · values random $0-100 · seed 97' and reveal muted line match.

claims.text: Second-price charges the lower of the two values. First-price winners pay only half their own value, but the winner holds the higher value.
claims.source: UNRECORDED CLAIM found by fact-checker (pass 22, 2026-10-14) in the reveal's second paragraph; sentence is the builder's, recorded here verbatim. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): DISPUTED. Read literally, first-price charges less than second-price. It does not: on average both charge $33.3 (c1, c2), and per auction, half the winner's value is below the lower value in 10,065 of the 20,000 seeded auctions (own node, mulberry32(97)), about half, as theory gives (P(max/2 < min) = 1/2). The sentence contradicts the lesson's own result. Fix (builder): compare each rule to the winner's value, not to the other rule, e.g. 'Second-price charges the lower of the two values. First-price winners bid only half their own value, but the winner is the higher value.' | Builder fix (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): W-211: reveal reworded along the fact-checker's suggestion; it no longer says first-price 'charges less' than second-price. Support: c3 (first-price optimal bid v/2, the winner pays its bid) and the winner being the higher-value bidder under every rule here. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Reveal para 2 (line 86) reads this sentence word for word. Per Demo payments(): second-price makes the winner pay min(a, b), the lower value. First-price makes the winner, the higher-value bidder (hi = max), pay hi/2, half its own value. The sentence no longer says first-price charges less than second-price, so it no longer contradicts the averages. Own re-run (mulberry32(97), 20,000 auctions): 33.395 / 33.303 / 33.302. Optimal first-price bid v/2 rests on c3 (verified, own best-response check).

recall.question: A seller switches from second-price to first-price sealed bids. Bidders' values come from the same spread and everyone bids optimally. What happens to the seller's average revenue?
options: It rises, because the winner now pays their own bid
It stays about the same, because bidders shade their bids
recall.why: Under first-price the winner pays their own bid, but bids are shaded (half the value here), so on average the seller collects the same as charging the lower value.
